title: Opportunity Zone designations for 2027: Find Every Client's 2026 Gain That Can Reach January 1, Price the December 31 Cliff, and Build the QOF 90% Test From the Books
excerpt: Treasury and the IRS published the Opportunity Zone designations for 2027 on November 5, 2026: 6,576 tracts, 2,594 rural, effective January 1. Here is how a CPA firm scans every client's books for 2026 gains, works out which ones can still reach the new five-year deferral and 10% or 30% step-up, prices the December 31 cliff per client, and sets up the fund's 90% test and the business's 50% income test from the ledger.
author: FinBoard Team
coverAlt: CPA reviewing sixty clients' QuickBooks gain accounts against the 2027 Opportunity Zone designations map, with a December 31 cliff timeline and a fund 90% asset test on screen
content:
Treasury and the IRS published the Opportunity Zone designations for 2027 on November 5, 2026: 6,576 tracts effective January 1. The work is not the map. It is finding every client gain realized in 2026 whose 180-day window reaches January 1, because a fund investment made in December gets no deferral and a January one gets five years.

Why this matters now

The IRS announced in IR-2026-132 on 2026-11-05 that Treasury has designated 6,576 census tracts as qualified opportunity zones, 2,594 of them rural, across all 50 states, the District of Columbia, and the territories. The designations take effect January 1, 2027 and run for ten years. The Treasury press release of the same day names the authority: the Working Families Tax Cuts, the 2025 law most practitioners still call OBBBA, made the incentive permanent, added enhanced benefits for rural tracts, and set a redesignation cycle every ten years. The full list and the interactive map are on the CDFI Fund site, updated 2026-11-05.

The designation date matters less than the regime change that arrives with it. For investments made through December 31, 2026, the IRS page on investing in a qualified opportunity fund, last updated December 23, 2025, still states the original rule: deferral lasts until December 31, 2026 or an earlier inclusion event, and only capital gains and qualified section 1231 gains recognized before January 1, 2027 can be deferred under it. For investments made after December 31, 2026, the law replaces that fixed date with a deferral that ends five years after the investment, restores a 10% basis step-up at five years, raises it to 30% for a qualified rural opportunity fund, and caps the appreciation exclusion at 30 years. Baker Tilly's year-end note of November 6, 2025 called 2026 the dead zone for a reason. A gain invested in December 2026 is recognized on the 2026 return anyway, with no step-up. The same gain invested in January 2027 is deferred to 2032 with 10% or 30% of it forgiven.

The trade press and the national firms have reported the designations, explained the two regimes, and mapped the tracts. The CPA Practice Advisor report of November 5 covers the count, the rural share, and the effective date. What none of it does is give a firm a repeatable way to find, across every client's books, which 2026 gains can still reach January 1, what the December cliff costs each one, and what the fund entities will owe the firm in bookkeeping once the money moves. That is this article.

Two regimes, one cliff: what a December investment gets and what a January investment gets

The table below is the whole decision in one place. Everything after it is about finding the gains and documenting the choice.

FeatureInvested on or before December 31, 2026Invested on or after January 1, 2027
Eligible gainCapital gain or qualified section 1231 gain recognized before January 1, 2027, invested within 180 days, not from a related partyThe same gain types, including 2026 gains whose 180-day window is still open in 2027
DeferralUntil December 31, 2026 or an earlier inclusion event, so a 2026 gain lands on the 2026 returnUntil the fifth anniversary of the investment or an earlier inclusion event
Basis step-up on the deferred gainNone reachable; the 10% and 15% steps required five and seven years of holding before the 2026 end date10% after five years; 30% in a qualified rural opportunity fund
Appreciation exclusionFull exclusion if the fund interest is held ten years, election available through 2047Full exclusion at ten years, with basis frozen at fair market value after 30 years
Where the fund can invest2018-designated tracts, which stay designated through December 31, 2028The 2027 tracts for ten years, plus 2018 tracts through 2028 under the Notice 2026-40 transition rules
Rural substantial improvement100% of basis50% of basis
ReportingForm 8997 for the investor, Form 8996 for the fundThe same forms, plus the new fund and zone business information returns the law added, with penalties for funds that miss them

The 180-day window is what decides which 2026 gains can wait. The period begins on the day the gain would be recognized and runs 180 days. A gain realized in the first week of July 2026 has its last day at the turn of the year, so for direct gains realized from about July 6, 2026 onward the window reaches January 1, 2027 on its own. Count the days for each sale date rather than trusting the rule of thumb. Gains realized earlier in 2026 and held directly by an individual, a trust, or a C corporation cannot wait. Their window closed in 2026, and the only choices were a 2026 investment for the ten-year exclusion alone or paying the tax.

Gains that flow through a partnership or an S corporation are different. The regulations let the owner start the 180 days on the day the entity sold, on the last day of the entity's tax year, or on the unextended due date of the entity's return. For a calendar-year partnership that is December 31, 2026 or March 15, 2027, which carries even a January 2026 gain to June 29, 2027 or September 11, 2027. Almost every 2026 pass-through gain can reach the new regime. Almost no early-2026 direct gain can.

One firm, sixty clients, every 2026 gain tested

Call the firm Harbor Street CPAs: sixty QuickBooks Online clients, four preparers, and a December already full of year-end bracket and section 179 projections. The figures are illustrative. The process is not.

Step one: pull the gain accounts from every client file

The query is the same for every client: every 2026 posting to Gain or Loss on Sale of Assets, Gain on Sale of Investments, and any Other Income account that received disposal proceeds, plus the fixed asset register for disposals with date, proceeds, and adjusted basis. Add the list of K-1s each client expects, because the partnership gains will not be in the client's own ledger until the K-1 arrives. Harbor Street found 14 clients with 2026 gains totaling $9.4 million across the sixty files. A firm that already runs one report across all of its client files gets this list in an afternoon. A firm opening sixty files one at a time does not.

Step two: strip what is not eligible

Only capital gain and qualified section 1231 gain can be deferred. Section 1245 depreciation recapture on equipment and vehicles is ordinary income and is out. So are inventory gains, ordinary business income, and any gain from a sale to a related party. A landscaping client sold a truck fleet for a $180,000 book gain; $150,000 of it is recapture on vehicles that had taken bonus depreciation, so $30,000 is eligible. After this pass, Harbor Street had 11 clients and $6.2 million of eligible gain.

Step three: bucket each gain by whether its window reaches January 1

Bucket A is direct gains realized before early July 2026: three clients, $1.1 million. Their windows closed in 2026. The firm's job is to confirm whether a fund investment was made, record the Form 8997 position, and move on. Bucket B is direct gains realized from July 6 through December 31: four clients, $2.3 million, with last days running from January 2 to June 29, 2027. Bucket C is pass-through gains realized at any point in 2026: four clients, $2.8 million. Each owner can elect the March 15, 2027 start date and has until September 11, 2027. Buckets B and C hold $5.1 million that can reach the new regime if nobody invests it in December.

Step four: price the cliff for each client

Dana, a Bucket B client, sold software company stock in September 2026 for a $400,000 long-term gain. At a combined federal rate of 23.8%, the 20% capital gains rate plus the 3.8% net investment income tax, the tax is $95,200. If she invests in a qualified opportunity fund in December 2026, the deferral ends December 31, 2026, so the $95,200 is due with her 2026 return in April 2027, there is no step-up, and the only remaining benefit is the exclusion of the fund interest's appreciation after ten years. If she invests the same $400,000 in January 2027, the gain is deferred to her 2032 return, and 10% of it, $40,000, is permanently excluded at five years, which saves $9,520 at the same rate. In a qualified rural opportunity fund the exclusion is 30%, $120,000, saving $28,560. The deferral itself keeps the remaining tax working for her for roughly six more years. State tax is a separate line, because not every state conforms to the federal deferral.

Step five: set up the books the fund will need

Two of the eleven clients plan to form their own fund rather than buy into a sponsored one. A self-formed fund is a partnership or corporation that files Form 8996 and must hold 90% of its assets in qualified opportunity zone property on the last day of its first six months and on the last day of its tax year. If it invests through a qualified opportunity zone business, that business must earn at least 50% of its gross income from activity in a zone, hold at least 70% of its tangible property as zone business property, keep nonqualified financial property under 5%, and shelter construction cash under a written 31-month working capital plan. The chart of accounts has to carry those categories as separate accounts from the first entry, and the firm has to close the books on each test date, not just at year-end.

Step six: the one-page memo

Each of the eleven clients gets one page: the gain, its source document, the eligible portion after recapture and related-party review, the three possible window start dates with the one elected, the last day to invest, the December and January outcomes side by side at the client's rates, the decision, and who made it. Harbor Street bills the memo as advisory work, because it is.

Accounting controls for Opportunity Zone designations and 2026 gains

Source data: each client's 2026 general ledger gain accounts and fixed asset disposal records with sale date, proceeds, and adjusted basis; brokerage 1099-B detail with trade dates; K-1s or draft K-1s with the entity's sale dates and tax year; the depreciation schedule for every disposed asset so recapture can be split from capital gain; the entity type and state of residence of each owner; the CDFI Fund list of 2027 tracts and the 2018 list that remains in force through 2028; Notice 2026-40 for property in tracts that were not redesignated; and, for any fund the firm will keep, the operating agreement, the written working capital plan, and the tax year.

Calculation: a fixed sequence anyone can rerun. Split each gain into ordinary recapture and eligible capital or section 1231 gain. Compute the 180-day window from each permitted start date and record the last day. Assign the bucket. For each eligible gain, compute the tax at the client's federal and state rates, the step-up at 10% or 30%, and the year the deferred gain will be recognized under each regime. The gain itself is a flow item of the 2026 tax year; the deferral only moves the year it is taxed. The fund investment is a point-in-time asset: debit Investment in Qualified Opportunity Fund, credit Cash, carried at cost on the books while its tax basis starts at zero because the deferred gain reduces it. For a C corporation investor that difference is a taxable temporary difference, so debit income tax expense and credit a deferred tax liability under ASC 740 for the deferred gain. For an individual there is no book entry for the deferral, only the Form 8997 schedule. The fund's 90% ratio is a balance sheet test on two dates; the business's 50% gross income test is a flow test over the year; the two must never be computed from the same report.

Review: a second preparer recounts the 180 days for every Bucket B gain from the trade date on the 1099-B, not from the settlement date; confirms the recapture split against the depreciation schedule; confirms no counterparty is a related party; confirms each target tract is on the November 5 list and whether it is rural; confirms the elected pass-through start date is one of the three the regulations allow; and confirms that no December 2026 investment was made for a gain that could have waited unless the memo records why. For a fund the firm keeps, the reviewer ties the June 30 and December 31 balance sheets to the 90% computation on Form 8996 and ties the gross income test to the full-year income statement.

Decision: the client owns whether to invest at all and in which fund, because the investment has to stand on its own before any tax benefit matters. The CPA owns the eligibility and timing memo, the window count, and the recapture split. The fund manager owns the 90% test and the working capital plan. The firm's partner owns the pricing of the memo as an advisory engagement and the decision to run the scan across every client rather than waiting for clients to ask.

Limits and common mistakes

The July 6 rule of thumb is a starting point, not an answer. The 180-day period begins on the day the gain would be recognized, and a one-day error puts a client on the wrong side of December 31. Count each one.

A ledger gain is not an eligible gain. On equipment and vehicle sales the recapture is often most of the number, and recapture is ordinary income. The scan finds candidates; the depreciation schedule decides what qualifies.

A December 2026 investment is not automatically a mistake. The ten-year exclusion on future appreciation is still available for investments in a fund holding property in a 2018 tract, and some clients will decide the investment itself justifies it. The mistake is making that choice without the memo showing what January would have given.

State conformity varies and some states do not follow the federal deferral at all. Price the state line separately for every client.

The regulations for the new regime are still being written. Notice 2026-55 asked for comments on the section 1400Z-2 rules by November 23, 2026, and the proposed information reporting rules for funds and zone businesses are still proposed. The deferral, step-up, and effective dates come from the statute and will not change; the mechanics around them may.

Harbor Street and Dana are illustrative. The tract counts, dates, and regime rules are from the IRS and Treasury announcements of November 5, 2026, the IRS program pages, and the Baker Tilly and Thomson Reuters explanations cited above.

Frequently Asked Questions

When do the new Opportunity Zone designations take effect, and what happens to the 2018 zones?

The 6,576 tracts Treasury and the IRS announced on November 5, 2026 become qualified opportunity zones on January 1, 2027 and keep that status for ten years. The tracts designated in 2018 stay in place through December 31, 2028, so the two sets overlap for 2027 and 2028. Notice 2026-40 sets transition rules for property in 2018 tracts that were not redesignated.

What does a client get by investing a 2026 gain in a qualified opportunity fund before December 31, 2026?

Only the ten-year exclusion on the fund investment's future appreciation. Under the original rules the deferral ends on December 31, 2026, so a 2026 gain invested in December is still reported on the 2026 return, and the 10% and 15% basis step-ups required five and seven years of holding before that date. An investment made in January 2027 instead defers the gain five years and earns a 10% step-up, or 30% in a qualified rural opportunity fund.

Can a gain realized in 2026 be invested in 2027 and still qualify for the five-year deferral?

Yes, if the 180-day investment window is still open on the investment date. The window starts on the day the gain is recognized, so a direct gain realized from about July 6, 2026 onward reaches January 1, 2027 on its own; count the days for each sale. For gains that pass through a partnership or S corporation, the owner may instead start the 180 days on the last day of the entity's tax year or on the unextended due date of its return, which carries any 2026 pass-through gain into 2027.

Which 2026 gains are not eligible for an opportunity zone investment?

Ordinary income is not eligible, and that includes section 1245 depreciation recapture on equipment and vehicle sales, inventory gains, and ordinary business income. Only the capital gain or qualified section 1231 gain portion qualifies, and gains from sales to related parties are excluded. On an equipment sale the recapture is often most of the gain, so the eligible amount is frequently far smaller than the general ledger gain account shows.

How does the 90% asset test work for a qualified opportunity fund, and what does it need from the books?

A fund must hold at least 90% of its assets in qualified opportunity zone property, measured on the last day of the first six months of its tax year and on the last day of the year. It is a point-in-time balance sheet test, so the books need separate accounts for qualified property, for interests in qualified opportunity zone businesses, and for cash and other nonqualified assets, with balances closed on each test date. The fund reports the result on Form 8996 and pays a penalty for each month it falls short.

Once the scan runs across every client file instead of waiting for the clients who happen to ask, the Opportunity Zone decision stops being a December phone call and becomes a dated memo with a window, a price, and an owner. FinBoard reads every client's QuickBooks file into one view, so a firm can pull the gain accounts and disposals across all of its clients at once, see each fund entity's balance sheet on its June 30 and December 31 test dates next to its full-year income statement, and drill from any figure to the postings behind it.
